incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using fake videos and social media profiles with his likeness to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals have created hundreds of fraudulent accounts offering immigration services that Leal never provides, often requesting $2,200 payments for fake residency assistance. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office last October, though the situation has dramatically worsened in recent months. His firm hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram.

The scam typically begins with AI-generated videos directing viewers to contact a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters exchange emails and send fake contracts to victims. Leal warns immigrants to be cautious of anyone requesting payments through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App, and to verify the identity of legal service providers online. He has changed his personal phone number due to the fraud and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the origin of the scams and launch a formal investigation.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article claimed that Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had an angry confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler over an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never actually occurred. This type of scam, which uses artificial intelligence to create deepfake content featuring well-known Australians, is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, along with politicians like Pauline Hanson and business figures including Alan Kohler and Dick Smith, are frequently impersonated in these schemes.

ASIC's enforcement efforts removed 19,400 scams last year, representing a 182 percent increase from the previous year. The regulator took down 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms. These schemes typically build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and reviews to establish credibility before targeting victims with scripted phone calls and requests for investment. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding alone do not indicate legitimacy.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, a smart ring company valued at eleven billion dollars, of falsely advertising the accuracy of its sleep tracking technology. The suit claims that Oura rings, which cost three hundred dollars and up, cannot accurately detect different sleep stages as marketed. Instead, the lawsuit alleges that the devices rely on artificial intelligence-generated guesses that are no better than a coin flip, despite Oura's claims of ninety-five percent sleep staging accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs.

Oura disputes these allegations, stating that it stands behind its scientific research and that its rings use multiple physiological signals to estimate sleep stages. The company notes that its sleep staging has been validated in multiple studies against polysomnography, the medical gold standard. However, experts emphasize that consumer sleep wearables provide only estimates and should not be viewed as medical devices or substitutes for clinical sleep studies. The lawsuit seeks class action status and a jury trial, though it remains unclear what compensation consumers might receive if the case proceeds or settles.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team identified a ransomware group called Aurora that has been active since April 2026, targeting organizations across multiple countries. The group developed a Linux variant of their ransomware capable of attacking ESXi virtual environments. Researchers discovered that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations between April and May 2026. The ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption and includes specific features to encrypt virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands.

The Aurora group also deployed custom tools to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers. Researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity affecting eight victim organizations across multiple countries, using different tactics including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to cloud storage. The investigation revealed multiple command and control servers, proxy servers, and infrastructure used by the group, along with technical indicators that can help organizations detect and defend against Aurora ransomware attacks.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas on May 6, claiming the chain's mandatory AI-powered delivery system called Dragontail caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across New York, New Jersey, Maryland, Washington DC, and Pennsylvania, alleges the system created operational problems when it gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen workflows. The franchisee says drivers began waiting up to 15 minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than delivering completed pizzas immediately, causing delays and customer dissatisfaction. In New York City, the company's year-over-year sales growth dropped from positive 10.19% to negative 9.78% after the rollout in 2024.

Chaac claims Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training on the system, ignored requests for support, and refused to modify the software despite worsening delivery metrics. The suit argues Pizza Hut breached its franchise agreement by mandating continued use of the problematic system. The company is seeking more than $100 million in damages plus attorneys' fees. Pizza Hut stated it would respond through appropriate legal channels but declined further comment. The lawsuit comes as Pizza Hut faces broader challenges, with its parent company Yum! Brands planning to close 250 US locations this year.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers have been sending personalized emails impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members of NPR's "Fresh Air" program to lure authors, entertainers and public figures into a fraudulent scheme. The messages appear legitimate, referencing the target's specific work and proposing interview topics, but eventually ask victims to pay fees ranging from around $250 for supposed production costs. Recipients including history professor Jennifer Black and comedian Bruce Vilanch initially believed the invitations were real opportunities before recognizing red flags like requests for payment and unusual procedures for a major production.

WHYY, NPR and law enforcement are investigating the scam, which cybersecurity experts say has become more sophisticated due to artificial intelligence making personalized impersonations cheaper and more convincing than traditional mass scams. The organizations clarify they never charge guests for interviews and warn people to verify requests through legitimate channels rather than responding to suspicious emails. Experts advise potential victims to watch for red flags like unprofessional email addresses, requests for money or personal credentials, and the unlikely scenario of a major host personally handling booking logistics.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
A fake American think tank funded by the Israeli government published over 560,000 words in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. The nonexistent Hanover Institute released 124 reports presenting pro-Israel arguments on topics including war crimes and genocide accusations, formatted as neutral academic research. The operation was part of a broader campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government through intermediaries, including the advertising company Havas Media, to manipulate how AI systems frame discussions about Israel.

The campaign involved multiple American firms working to seed websites and content into training data used by major chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude. Israeli officials have expressed frustration about the public diplomacy efforts, with some calling them wasteful, as American public opinion has increasingly turned toward sympathy for Palestinians. While the AI influence operations appear to be working technically, reshaping chatbot responses, they have not reversed declining American support for Israeli policies, with recent polling showing record low approval ratings for Israel among Americans.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, and Warner Music, have sued AI music generators Udio and Suno, claiming they illegally scraped thousands of copyrighted songs to train their systems. The labels allege that both companies copied music en masse without permission or compensation and that their models directly reproduce sections of famous songs. The lawsuits name artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others whose work was allegedly used. The record labels submitted a lengthy list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were scraped.

To support their claims, the labels created AI-generated songs using specific prompts and demonstrated that the outputs closely resemble existing copyrighted recordings. For example, prompts requesting 1950s rock and roll style produced songs nearly identical to Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," and a prompt describing Mariah Carey's characteristics generated a near-perfect copy of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits were filed separately in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, setting up a major legal battle about generative AI services and copyright infringement.

Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve disputes over copyright infringement. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs, including The Temptations' "My Girl," to train its artificial intelligence system without permission. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs through AI technology. Financial terms were not disclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first major licensing agreement with a major music label and reflects the growing tension between entertainment companies and AI startups over training data. UMG's CEO stated the deal demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies. Udio's CEO expressed enthusiasm about collaborating with UMG to advance AI in music creation. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false holdings in court filings for a lawsuit involving homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga. The homeowner sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire in her Carson home left it uninhabitable, and subsequent storm damage delayed repairs. Despite efforts to rebuild, the work was never completed, leading Meni-Siliga and her husband to drain savings, declare bankruptcy, and lose their home to foreclosure. A State Farm attorney acknowledged that a colleague used an AI tool called Irys, believing it would verify legal citations, but it failed to catch seven nonexistent case citations across eight filings.

The incident highlights growing concerns about AI use in law, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments now using generative AI. A database tracking legal hallucinations worldwide has documented 1,922 cases, mostly in the United States. Last year, a California attorney received a record ten thousand dollar fine for using ChatGPT in a brief containing fabricated quotes. State Farm stated it expects its external counsel to maintain the highest ethical standards and verify accuracy in all legal filings. The case is scheduled for trial in October.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI gaining popularity in Kenya for affordability, performance, customization-Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Chinese artificial intelligence models are becoming increasingly popular among Kenyan developers and technology companies due to their lower costs, strong performance, and customizable open-source nature. According to recent analysis, Chinese AI models represented roughly half of all AI use on OpenRouter, a platform offering about 400 models, up from less than 25 percent a year prior. On Hugging Face, another major AI platform, Chinese models made up 19 of the 25 most-downloaded open-source systems. Kenyan companies are using Chinese models like DeepSeek and Qwen for applications in legal technology, business intelligence, document processing, and coding.

Local developers and company leaders cite cost efficiency and computing power requirements as major advantages. Kenya has limited GPU supply, making models requiring fewer computing resources easier to deploy locally. Experts note that Chinese models now perform comparably to leading Western models while consuming fewer tokens. The ability to download and retrain these open-weight models with local data allows Kenyan developers to customize them for local languages and industry-specific needs without building models from scratch. Qhala and other Kenyan companies are exploring how these models could support healthcare diagnostics and disaster prevention systems adapted for African communities.

stories.Headline: EU places ChatGPT, Reddit, Roblox under strictest platform rules
stories.Summary:
The European Union has classified ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine and designated Reddit and Roblox as Very Large Online Platforms under its Digital Services Act. These three American companies will now face direct supervision from the European Commission and must comply with stricter requirements designed to address risks related to children, election integrity, and public security. The rules apply to services with over 45 million users in the EU, bringing the total number of regulated platforms to 28.

Companies failing to meet the new requirements within four months face fines up to 6 percent of their annual global revenue. Reddit reported 57.2 million EU users in July, while Roblox has 46.6 million. OpenAI stated it would prepare to meet ChatGPT's additional obligations, and Roblox welcomed the designation, emphasizing safety's importance. This designation adds another regulatory layer for ChatGPT, which already complies with the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act.

stories.Headline: CSA's Top Cloud Threats: Identity, AI -- Campus Technology
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance surveyed 507 security professionals to identify the top threats to cloud computing in 2026. Identity and access management issues rose to the number one concern, moving up from second place in 2024, while misconfiguration dropped to fifth. Two artificial intelligence-related threats appeared in the rankings for the first time, including AI-enhanced attacks and AI system compromise. The top eleven threats also include insecure third-party resources, insecure APIs, advanced persistent threats, and inadequate cloud security strategy and governance.

The survey results reveal a significant shift in the cloud threat landscape, with organizations now prioritizing identity protection, artificial intelligence risks, and software supply chains over infrastructure-focused concerns. Security scores ranged closely from 7.95 for identity and access management to 7.45 for system vulnerabilities. The report aims to help organizations make informed risk-management decisions about cloud adoption by providing expert analysis of technical and business impacts, real-world examples, and corresponding security controls across cloud and AI environments.

stories.Headline: What We Know About Haryana Police's AI Task Force.
stories.Summary:
Haryana Police is establishing an Artificial Intelligence Task Force to expand AI use in law enforcement operations. An Indian Police Service officer will lead the initiative, which focuses on cybercrime investigations, financial transaction analysis, complaint management and court information processing. The police emphasized that AI will support human investigators rather than replace them, with officers responsible for verifying leads and making final decisions.

The task force will build on existing technology systems Haryana Police already uses, including a 2022 facial recognition program that deactivated nearly 1,000 fraudulent SIM cards and current cybercrime helplines. The police plan to implement safeguards around accuracy, transparency, data security and human oversight, though specific implementation details remain unclear. Haryana Police has not disclosed how it will test systems, measure errors, conduct audits or handle incorrect results, and has not explained how new AI capabilities will integrate with current infrastructure or whether it plans to use facial recognition or predictive policing technologies.

stories.Headline: Who Writes AI's Rules When Someone Else Owns the Machines?
stories.Summary:
# Summary

South Africa withdrew its Draft National AI Policy in April 2026 after discovering that at least six of its 67 academic references were fabricated, highlighting a broader challenge facing the Global South. The incident underscores a critical debate about who controls artificial intelligence governance and infrastructure. Currently, the United States and China host roughly 86% of global data centre capacity, giving them power to set rules and prices for AI systems worldwide. This concentration of computing power represents what critics call "tech colonialism," where developing nations provide data and demand but lack ownership and control over the technology itself.

BRICS countries and other Global South nations are attempting to shift AI governance away from Western-led standards by emphasizing digital sovereignty and development rights. They are seeking to anchor AI governance within the United Nations rather than OECD-led bodies and have established organizations like the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. However, meaningful sovereignty requires owning physical infrastructure, not just adopting policies. The article notes that until developing nations build regional computing capacity and chip manufacturing capabilities, they remain dependent on foreign platforms controlled by American hyperscalers or Chinese firms. True sovereignty means choosing dependencies rather than having them imposed.

stories.Headline: 《TAIPEI TIMES》 Taiwan aims to train 500,000 AI pros by 2040 - 焦點
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's government plans to invest over 40 billion Taiwan dollars, approximately 1.26 billion US dollars, to develop 10 major artificial intelligence projects next year. President William Lai has set an ambitious goal to train at least 500,000 AI professionals by 2040. The administration launched the AI Talent Ark Project this year to nurture talent through fundamental education, professional development, and data-driven approaches, aiming to build a large AI talent pool and strengthen Taiwan's competitiveness in technology sectors.

The government is also prioritizing technological sovereignty and national resilience. The Minister of Digital Affairs announced plans to accumulate at least 10,000 graphics processing units through private investment in AI computing centers within a year. Taiwan is focusing on developing sovereign AI systems that understand Taiwanese perspectives and languages, along with low-Earth-orbit satellite communications to ensure independent communication capabilities. Officials emphasized that technological sovereignty means focusing on critical technologies rather than developing every technology domestically.

stories.Summary:
Paisabazaar, India's leading financial products marketplace, reports that artificial intelligence now generates approximately 86 percent of new code written on its platform. The company's Chief Technology Officer emphasized that the objective is not to eliminate engineers but to enhance their productivity by automating repetitive tasks. This shift allows engineers to focus on architecture, problem-solving and innovation while accelerating development velocity and enabling teams to pursue a larger product roadmap.

The financial services company is expanding its engineering team despite increased AI involvement, demonstrating its commitment to using productivity gains for expansion rather than workforce reduction. AI-assisted development is integrated throughout the engineering lifecycle, including code writing, testing, debugging and documentation. The company plans to continue deepening AI adoption across both engineering and consumer-facing experiences to expand innovation, improve productivity and deliver more personalized financial services at scale.

stories.Headline: Dyna.Ai Selected as Technology Partner in Hong Kong's GenA.I. Sandbox++
stories.Summary:
Dyna.Ai, a Singapore-based AI company, has been selected as a technology partner in Hong Kong's new GenA.I. Sandbox++ program, marking its second consecutive selection by Hong Kong financial regulators. The sandbox was jointly launched by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Securities and Futures Commission, Insurance Authority, and Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority in collaboration with Cyberport. Out of nearly 100 regional proposals, 36 use cases involving 30 financial institutions and 27 technology providers were chosen, including major institutions like Bank of China (Hong Kong) and Manulife (International), alongside technology partners Google, IBM, and Dyna.Ai.

Unlike earlier programs focused on generative AI banking pilots, Sandbox++ expands across banking, insurance, securities, and pension funds to test Agentic AI systems that execute complex tasks under real-time governance. Dyna.Ai will demonstrate how financial institutions can safely delegate workflow execution to autonomous AI agents while maintaining strict oversight and compliance. The company plans to showcase its solutions and governance frameworks at LEAP 2026 in Riyadh later this year.

stories.Headline: Brazil archbishop establishes rules for use of AI in archdiocesan communications
stories.Summary:
Archbishop Josafá Menezes da Silva of Aracaju, Brazil has created guidelines for artificial intelligence use within his archdiocese. The rules require all AI-generated content to undergo human review before publication and to be clearly labeled to distinguish it from human-created work. The archbishop based these directives on Church teachings about human dignity and Pope Leo XIV's messages about AI's potential to create false realities and deepfakes.

The guidelines prohibit clergy from using AI to recreate their appearance, voice, or simulate statements they never made. However, AI can serve as an auxiliary tool for creating backgrounds, textures, illustrations, and assisting with visual composition. The archbishop emphasized that all Church communications must remain truthful and responsible, urging pastoral workers and the faithful to consult with church leadership when using technology to ensure it serves the Church's mission.

stories.Headline: China promotes coordinated development of data industry, artificial intelligence-- Beijing Review
stories.Summary:
# Summary

China's data industry reached 6.78 trillion yuan in 2025, and the country is now focusing on coordinating development between its data sector and artificial intelligence capabilities. The 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo, held in Guiyang from August 28-30, attracted 372 companies and over 16,000 guests to showcase innovations in computing power, large models, and data circulation. Government officials emphasized that high-quality datasets are essential for advancing AI capabilities and that data technology is transforming traditional industries like power generation and renewable energy forecasting.

Beyond upgrading existing industries, data and AI are creating new business opportunities and employment categories. Companies are hiring data collectors to train robots through embodied intelligence projects, while micro-enterprises and one-person startups are emerging as signs of entrepreneurial growth. International participants from Zimbabwe, Chile, Pakistan, and other nations attended to explore cooperation opportunities, with officials highlighting the potential for shared benefits and technological exchange between countries through collaborative data and AI development.
